deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two unrelated groups of work: a number-theoretic computation at the top and potential-theory / complex-function sketches (mostly rotated) below.

(A) Primes in the two classes mod 4 (top of page).
Set a = ∞ and write
  lim_{a→∞} [ Σ_{p<a} log(1 − 1/p^s) + Σ_{q<a} log(1 + 1/q^s) ] = D.

My interpretation (not written on the page): p runs over primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) and q over primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), with χ the non-principal character mod 4. Then
  Σ log(1 − χ(p) p^{-s}) = −log L(s, χ),
with L(s, χ) = 1 − 3^{-s} + 5^{-s} − ... . So D = −log L(s, χ), and at s = 1 this is −log(π/4).

Riemann's question is whether the partial Euler product converges at the boundary point s = 1.

Step 1. Expand each logarithm to first order: log(1 ∓ x) = ∓x + O(x²). The quadratic terms give an absolutely convergent series, Σ O(1/p²). The convergence question therefore reduces to
  −Σ_{p<a} 1/p + Σ_{q<a} 1/q.

Step 2. Each one-sided sum diverges. To see how fast, he estimates a block Σ_{a<q<b} 1/q. He assumes primes have density 1/log x and that half of them are ≡ 3 (mod 4) (a heuristic of Gauss–Legendre type plus Dirichlet equidistribution). This gives
  Σ_{a<q<b} 1/q ≈ (1/2) ∫_a^b dx / (x log x)
                = (1/2)(log log b − log log a)
                = (1/2) log( log b / log a ).

Conclusion: each class contributes (1/2) log log x + O(1). The leading terms cancel in the difference, and convergence of the difference depends on finer information about the error terms. This is the problem later settled by Mertens (1874) and by the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions.

(B) Potential theory / Dirichlet integral (rotated fragments).
- Laplace equation: ∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² = 0.
- Complex form: u + vi = f(x + yi), and α + βi = f(x + yi), with a Cauchy–Riemann relation ∂α/∂x − ∂β/∂y = 0.
- Dirichlet integral: ∫∫ [(∂u/∂x)² + (∂u/∂y)²] dx dy.
- The same integrand in polar coordinates: [(∂u/∂r)² + (1/r²)(∂u/∂θ)²] r dr dθ.
- He tests the integral near a singular point: ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^ρ (α²/r²) r dr dθ. This integrand arises from a logarithmic or angular singularity, e.g. u = α log r or u = αθ. The integral equals 2πα² ∫ dr/r and diverges logarithmically at r = 0.
- Other fragments: α/ρ; terms of the shape αr/(x+yi) + αr/(x−yi) (a pole / real-part construction); factors (z − a) and (z − a)u for removing a singularity at z = a.
- Sketches of simply and multiply connected regions with marked interior points (poles/branch points) and a cut ('Const.', a long slit).

This is the circle of ideas of the Dirichlet principle and the 1851 dissertation (Grundlagen ...). The previous page carries 'B Riemann, stud math', which suggests a student-period notebook (late 1840s – c. 1851).

There is also a rotated fragment 'Σ_1^∞ (n/·)', possibly a Legendre/Jacobi-symbol sum; it is too unclear to reconstruct.
errors: Step A.2 is heuristic. Using density 1/(2 log x) for primes ≡ 3 mod 4 presupposes the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions, which was unproved at the time. It gives the correct leading term, (1/2) log log, as later confirmed by Mertens and de la Vallée Poussin. It does not by itself prove that the difference −Σ 1/p + Σ 1/q converges; that needs error-term control (Mertens 1874).
The identity of p and q as the two residue classes mod 4 is not stated on the page. It is inferred from the signs (1 − p^{-s}) versus (1 + q^{-s}) and the factor 1/2.

In (B) the integral of α²/r² · r over a disc around 0 diverges. If this was meant as an energy of a singular function, the singularity must be excised, ∫_ε^ρ. Riemann presumably notes the divergence; it is not an error on the page as written.

results.what: Reduction of convergence of the Euler product for L(s, χ_4) at s = 1 to the convergence of −Σ 1/p + Σ 1/q over the two residue classes mod 4
results.modern_name: Convergence of Euler product of Dirichlet L-function on the line Re s = 1; Mertens' theorem Σ χ(p)/p converges
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1837) for L-series and Euler products; Mertens (1874) for convergence of Σ χ(p)/p and the Euler product at s = 1

results.what: Heuristic Σ_{a<q<b, q≡3 mod 4} 1/q ≈ (1/2) log(log b / log a) via prime density 1/log x split equally between classes
results.modern_name: Mertens' second theorem in arithmetic progressions: Σ_{p≤x, p≡a mod q} 1/p = (1/φ(q)) log log x + O(1)
results.usually_credited_to: Mertens 1874 (rigorous); Gauss/Legendre density heuristic; Dirichlet equidistribution

results.what: Laplace equation, Cauchy–Riemann relations, Dirichlet integral in Cartesian and polar form, and test of a logarithmic singularity's energy
results.modern_name: Dirichlet principle / harmonic functions with prescribed singularities

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's interest in Euler products and prime distribution is well known. Using the density 1/log x for primes in a progression is a natural Gauss/Dirichlet-style heuristic. The mildly notable points are: (i) the sheet may date from his student period, given 'stud math' on the facing page, which would place him thinking about the boundary convergence of L(1, χ_4)'s Euler product before 1859; and (ii) he anticipates the (1/2) log log heuristic behind Mertens' 1874 result. Nothing is proven rigorously, and the potential-theory material is standard Riemann dissertation content.

checkable.sympy: integrate(1/(x*log(x)), (x, a, b), conds='none').simplify()  # with a,b>1 positive
checkable.asserts: ∫_a^b dx/(x log x) = log(log b) − log(log a)
(1/2)(log log b − log log a) = (1/2) log(log b / log a)
log(1 − 1/p) = −1/p + O(1/p²), so the quadratic remainder is absolutely summable over primes
L(1, χ_4) = π/4, so D = −log L(1, χ_4) = log(4/π) at s = 1 under the mod-4 interpretation
The Dirichlet integral of a log/angular singularity over an annulus equals 2π α² log(ρ/ε), diverging as ε→0
For u = α log r, |∇u|² = α²/r², matching the integrand on the page
